title: Behavioural Requirements Definition
excerpt: Behavioural requirements definition specifies testable interface-level behaviour for systems that use AI outputs or other uncertain operational inputs. The practice separates product behaviour from model behaviour and makes human, system, and governance boundaries explicit.
metaDescription: Defines interface-level behavioural requirements for AI outputs, governance review, human oversight, and non-AI operational systems.
summary: Behavioural requirements definition turns trust, oversight, governance, and operational constraints into specific interface-level requirements. It defines what the product must show, prevent, record, and require from users when AI outputs or other uncertain inputs affect action.
definition: Behavioural requirements definition is the practice of producing specific, testable interface-level requirements that define what a product must do, must not do, and must hand over to human judgement when AI outputs or other uncertain operational inputs are involved.
keyFacts: Behavioural requirements are interface requirements, not model requirements.
The practice produces positive requirements, constraint requirements, and boundary requirements.
A well-formed behavioural requirement is testable, interface-level, connected to a governance or trust rationale, and explicit about the human and system boundary.
The practice is used after trust-and-oversight analysis and before human-AI interaction design begins.
In AI-enabled products, behavioural requirements specify what the interface shows, prevents, logs, and requires when AI outputs are involved.
Callsign examples include attributable fraud control decisions, timestamped policy modifications, and interface-only reconstruction of historical decision logic.
Puraite examples include blinded review mode, visible text evidence, numerical confidence with colour coding, and override interaction parity.
Owkin K examples include visible data sources, out-of-scope query disclosure, and capability scope communication at entry.
The practice is not AI-scoped; KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and the handheld command-and-control engagement are non-AI evidence for behavioural requirements.
KISPE verification vocabulary refers to specified tests, not executed tests.
bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Behavioural requirements definition specifies what a product interface must do when AI outputs or other uncertain operational inputs affect user action. The practice turns trust calibration problems, oversight needs, governance obligations, and operational constraints into testable product requirements.

A behavioural requirement is not a broad principle such as trustworthy AI or human oversight. It is a specific statement about product behaviour, such as requiring confidence information beside an AI recommendation, requiring evidence visibility at the point of use, preventing untracked policy modification, or requiring an explicit confirm action before an AI-influenced action is carried out.

Behavioural requirements are interface-level requirements. They do not specify model performance. A requirement such as the model must achieve 95 percent accuracy is a model requirement. A requirement such as the interface must display confidence level alongside every model recommendation is a behavioural requirement.

## What behavioural requirements definition does

Behavioural requirements definition produces specific, testable requirements for how the interface handles AI outputs, human decisions, system states, evidence, policy changes, uncertainty, and governance review.

The practice produces three categories of requirement:

- Positive requirements specify what the system must do, such as display AI confidence, show supporting evidence, log decisions, surface the data source, or trigger confirmation for AI-influenced actions above a consequence threshold.
- Constraint requirements specify what the system must not do, such as display AI recommendations before independent human assessment where epistemic independence is required, allow untracked modification to live AI policy during evaluation, or produce outputs without surfacing the data they are based on.
- Boundary requirements specify where human judgement takes over from AI recommendation, including the workflow points where a human must make an active decision rather than accept a default and the interactions that enforce that boundary.

The practice is most explicit in AI-enabled products because model behaviour cannot be fully specified in advance. The product behaviour can still be specified: what the interface shows, when it shows it, what users can do with AI outputs, what the interface must prevent, and what evidence governance reviewers need to see.

## Well-formed behavioural requirements are testable, interface-level, justified, and boundary-explicit

A well-formed behavioural requirement can be assessed as met or not met without ambiguity. A statement such as the AI should be helpful is not a behavioural requirement. A statement such as the AI data source must be visible on the same screen as its output is a behavioural requirement because it can be checked against an interface.

A well-formed behavioural requirement specifies product behaviour at the interface level. Model behaviour is not fully under design control. The interface handling of model outputs is under design control.

A well-formed behavioural requirement is connected to a governance or trust rationale. The requirement should trace back to an identified trust calibration problem, an oversight requirement, or a governance obligation. Without that rationale, a requirement is only a preference.

A well-formed behavioural requirement is explicit about responsibility boundaries. A stronger requirement states that the AI recommends, the human decides, and the interface enforces that boundary by requiring an explicit confirm action before any AI recommendation is acted on.

## When behavioural requirements definition is used

Behavioural requirements definition is used after trust-and-oversight analysis has identified trust calibration failures and oversight gaps. Trust-and-oversight analysis identifies what must be addressed. Behavioural requirements definition specifies what the design must implement to address it.

Behavioural requirements definition is used before human-AI interaction design begins. The requirements constrain and direct design work rather than being written retrospectively after interface decisions have already been made.

Behavioural requirements definition is used in governance-sensitive contexts, including enterprise banking, regulated medical devices, clinical research, and institutional AI deployments. In these contexts, behavioural requirements can become formal documents that governance reviewers can assess against.

## Callsign fraud detection evidence for policy-layer behavioural requirements

In the Callsign fraud detection case, the model and policy separation functioned as behavioural requirements implemented through architecture. The policy layer specified what the interface must do with fraud model outputs, including threshold application, step-up authentication triggers, decision logging, and policy history visibility.

The documented Callsign requirements included that every fraud control decision resulting in a block or step-up authentication had to be attributable to a named, reviewable policy accessible within the same interface session, without requiring an engineering query. This was a governance traceability requirement.

The documented Callsign requirements also included timestamped and user-attributed policy modification tracking. The evaluation environment was not allowed to support untracked live modification, making this a constraint requirement.

A further Callsign requirement stated that risk analysts had to be able to reconstruct complete decision logic for any historical event using only the interface, without system logs or backend access. This requirement defined the human review boundary.

These Callsign requirements came from governance consumer analysis of what bank risk teams under SCA and PCI DSS compliance needed to verify. Lloyds Bank and HSBC contracts followed demos that demonstrated these requirements met.

## Puraite AI systematic review evidence for epistemic independence requirements

In the Puraite AI systematic review case, behavioural requirements were used to protect epistemic independence. Each reviewer inclusion or exclusion decision had to reflect the reviewer evaluation of the evidence, not a response to an AI decision shown too early.

The blinded mode requirement stated that the AI inclusion or exclusion decision must not be visible to the reviewer before the reviewer had recorded an independent decision. This is a constraint requirement because it prevents anchoring before independent assessment.

The confidence requirement stated that when AI decisions are shown, the confidence level must be expressed as a numerical percentage with colour coding rather than as a binary include or exclude recommendation. This is a positive requirement because uncertainty becomes a first-class interface element.

The evidence availability requirement stated that the text evidence used by the AI must be visible in the review interface from the outset without requiring interaction. The override requirement stated that override must require no more interaction than acceptance, so that the non-default path is cognitively equivalent to the default. Together, these requirements specify evidence access and genuine optionality at the human decision boundary.

## Owkin K evidence for data-boundary transparency requirements

In the Owkin K biomedical AI case, the central behavioural requirement was data boundary transparency. Users needed to understand what K knew, and what K did not know, in order to trust outputs appropriately.

One requirement stated that every K output must display the data sources it drew upon in terms legible to researchers and without requiring navigation away from the output. This is a positive requirement because provenance is visible at the point of use.

A second requirement stated that K must not respond to queries outside its data boundary without explicitly communicating that the query is outside scope. K must not produce outputs that appear knowledge-based when they are actually inference without data support. This is a constraint requirement.

A third requirement stated that the entry point must communicate K capability scope before users invest in framing questions. This is a positive requirement for capability transparency at entry.

## Non-AI behavioural requirements evidence from KISPE Space

Behavioural requirements definition is not limited to AI systems. KISPE Space had no model, no inference, and no recommendation behaviour in the material relevant to this practice.

The KISPE Space engagement produced 61 behavioural rules in ten families: geographic and workspace context, time, imagery, satellite services, provenance and uncertainty, notifications, connectivity, briefings, integration and diagnostics, and field presentation. Each rule carried four parts: trigger, required response, guard, and verification check.

The guard field is the important requirement form in the KISPE Space material. It states what the behaviour must not do, which distinguishes these behavioural rules from ordinary acceptance criteria.

The KISPE Space material also included six state models and eight cross-module regression checks covering area confirmation and query lineage, imagery catalogue and asset retrieval, provider reachability and device observations, local annotation synchronisation, saved live view versus frozen briefing, and notification interaction.

The KISPE Space verification vocabulary must be read as specified tests, not executed tests. The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and did not compare the built interface against the delivered designs.

## Non-AI behavioural requirements evidence from Raymarine marine radio work

The Raymarine fixed-mount VHF engagement produced close to two hundred acceptance checks across the specification set. These included checks on the physical control contract, detailed voice operating flows, calling specification, AIS information hierarchy, event priority matrix, emergency specification, exception catalogue, radio and chartplotter responsibility model, UI acceptance criteria at handover, and UI specification checks.

Each Raymarine acceptance check was written as an observable condition testable against a prototype, hardware mockup, or firmware implementation, not as a subjective preference.

Four Raymarine design rules were locked for UI delivery and written as acceptance conditions: no screen view remaps radio tuning or direct safety controls; communication and system states must reflect the actual protocol and data state; severity is prioritised while current context is preserved and restorable; and a disconnected chartplotter cannot disable local radio functions.

The Raymarine contribution to behavioural requirements definition is the formulation: a requirement names what must be true on screen, under a named starting condition, after a named action. The radio was built and released. No design-fidelity comparison is recorded.

## Non-AI behavioural requirements evidence from Schone Airspace Group Mission Control

The Schone Airspace Group Mission Control engagement produced twelve principal interaction contracts. Each contract specified the initiating action, state transition, visible result, required source inputs, exception behaviour, and conditions by which the design could be checked.

The Schone engagement also produced eight operational invariants as the binding acceptance core of the interaction specification. UI styling and component substitution had to preserve these invariants.

The invariant formulation is the contribution to behavioural requirements definition. It creates a short list of rules that survive visual change and lets a component swap be tested against the interaction contract.

The Schone product was built and is in test, not deployed. The fidelity comparison for Schone belongs to its own case material and is not used as evidence on this practice page.

## Non-AI behavioural requirements evidence from handheld command-and-control work

The handheld command-and-control engagement for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority, and clarity of operator control. The engagement did not extend to autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, or any certification or weapons-review activity.

Creative Navy designed the surface through which a human supervises the system. Creative Navy did not design the system. The deliverables were led and co-authored with the client design team, not delivered by Creative Navy alone.

The behaviour model separated vehicle status, mission segment, guidance mode, armament state, command state, system health, and alert priority. These categories were related but not interchangeable. Vehicle status described what the vehicle was doing, mission segment described where the mission was, and health and alerts described what was wrong.

The central behavioural rule was that a requested state must not visually replace a confirmed state before the vehicle reports the result. This is a behavioural requirement because it specifies what the interface may and may not display while a system state is pending.

The engagement also specified armament state as five values: safe, armed, change pending, unavailable, unknown. It specified command state as seven values: requested, sending, awaiting acknowledgement, accepted, rejected, timed out, resulting state confirmed. It specified alert priority as three levels with response expectations attached: warning required immediate awareness and immediate response, caution required immediate awareness but a less urgent response, and advisory required awareness with later action possibly necessary.

The governing discipline was to use only states the technical system can actually determine. That rule bounds behavioural requirements by what the system can know.

The model purpose was practical checking: every piece of information and every control could be tested against a clear operator question, assigned an operational priority, and classified as persistent, contextual, or alert-driven. Information that could not answer one of those questions became a candidate for removal, consolidation, or secondary placement.

This handheld interface was built. The product contains object detection, confidence scoring, and target suggestion, but Creative Navy did not design the model behaviour, trust calibration, or override semantics for those functions.

## Relationship to model requirements

Behavioural requirements are interface requirements, not model requirements. The distinction is necessary because model requirements specify model performance, while behavioural requirements specify product behaviour around model outputs.

A model requirement may state that a model must reach a performance threshold. A behavioural requirement states how the interface must handle model outputs, such as displaying confidence, showing provenance, requiring explicit confirmation, or preventing premature exposure of a recommendation.

Model requirements are the responsibility of the ML team. Behavioural requirements are the responsibility of the design team. Behavioural requirements definition sits at the boundary between governance and design by translating trust and oversight findings into product requirements that the interface must implement.

## Outputs of behavioural requirements definition

Behavioural requirements definition produces requirements that can be used by designers, governance reviewers, engineering teams, and product teams. The output is not a general design principle. It is a requirement set that can be checked against an interface, prototype, policy layer, or implementation.

Typical outputs include positive requirements, constraint requirements, boundary requirements, state rules, guard conditions, acceptance checks, interaction contracts, operational invariants, and verification checks. The exact format depends on the system and domain.

The strongest requirements name the starting condition, the action or trigger, the required visible response, the guard or prohibited behaviour, and the condition by which the behaviour can be checked.

## Boundaries and limits of the practice

Behavioural requirements definition does not specify model performance and does not replace ML evaluation. It specifies interface behaviour around model outputs and other uncertain system inputs.

The non-AI evidence on this page must not be treated as AI evidence. KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and the handheld command-and-control engagement had no model, no inference, and no recommendations in the material used for this practice page.

The KISPE Space verification and regression vocabulary identifies specified tests, not executed tests. The page does not claim that KISPE Space testing was completed.

The Raymarine radio was built and released, and the KISPE Space and handheld interfaces were built, but no shipped-as-designed or design-fidelity claim is made for KISPE Space, Raymarine, or the handheld command-and-control engagement. The Schone product was built and is in test, not deployed.

This practice page does not claim safety, certification, weapons-review, airworthiness, type-approval, or regulatory credentials for KISPE Space, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, or the handheld command-and-control engagement. NASA, FAA, and EASA guidance framed categories in the handheld command-and-control work, but Creative Navy did not certify to, audit against, or work to those standards.

No evidence on this page establishes that any requirement set prevented an error, accident, wrong command, or adverse outcome. The documented evidence establishes what the interface was required to do.

## Related practices

Behavioural requirements definition follows trust-and-oversight analysis for AI. Trust-and-oversight analysis identifies trust calibration and governance problems. Behavioural requirements definition specifies what the design must do to address them.

Behavioural requirements definition directly informs decision boundary design. Boundary requirements are one category of behavioural requirement, and decision boundary design implements those boundaries in workflow and interaction structure.

Behavioural requirements definition also supports behavioural governance for AI products by producing the requirements that governance-sensitive AI product design must implement and expose for review.
